explanations.answer: The Day of the Lord has already come
explanations.explanation: That's the claim Paul warns about. He asks the brothers not to be easily disconcerted or alarmed by any spirit or message or letter seeming to be from him and his team, alleging that the Day of the Lord has already come (2 Thessalonians 2:2). A letter with a famous name at the bottom isn't always from that person, friend.

explanations.answer: The Day of the Lord will come next spring
explanations.explanation: Paul never gives a season, friend. The claim he's pushing back on is that the Day of the Lord has already come (2 Thessalonians 2:2). And naming a date is a bold move, since Jesus says that no one knows the day or the hour (Matthew 24:36). I once tried guessing when my timer would go off and I was wrong every single time.

explanations.answer: The Day of the Lord will never come
explanations.explanation: Nope, it's the opposite direction. The claim Paul names is that the Day of the Lord has already come (2 Thessalonians 2:2). He asks the brothers not to be easily disconcerted or alarmed by a message like that.

I get why this one tempts you, because Paul is talking about that very claim. But he's warning against it, not agreeing with it. He says, "Let no one deceive you in any way, for it will not come until the rebellion occurs and the man of lawlessness—the son of destruction—is revealed." (2 Thessalonians 2:3) So Paul puts those two things before the Day of the Lord.

That's right. Paul warns the brothers about any spirit or message or letter alleging that the Day of the Lord has already come (2 Thessalonians 2:2), and he tells them not to be deceived. He says "…it will not come until the rebellion occurs and the man of lawlessness—the son of destruction—is revealed." (2 Thessalonians 2:3) The warning is the whole point of his letter here.

Yes, he'll go as high as it gets. He will "…exalt himself above every so-called god or object of worship." proclaiming himself to be God (2 Thessalonians 2:4). That's the biggest claim a person could make, and it's a false one. Paul wants the brothers to know it ahead of time.

A prophet is too small a claim for this one, friend. Paul says he will oppose and exalt himself above every so-called god or object of worship, proclaiming himself to be God (2 Thessalonians 2:4). He's not going for a speaking role. He's going for the top spot.

An angel is not God, so that's aiming too low. Paul says he will exalt himself above every so-called god or object of worship, so he proclaims himself to be God (2 Thessalonians 2:4). Nothing less than that will do for him.
That's it. Paul says, "So he will seat himself in the temple of God, proclaiming himself to be God." (2 Thessalonians 2:4) He doesn't pick some random spot. He sits down right where God is worshiped.

Babylon doesn't show up in Paul's words here. Paul says the man of lawlessness will seat himself in the temple of God (2 Thessalonians 2:4). A palace would be the place for a king, but Paul names the temple.

Pharaoh, the king of Egypt, doesn't show up in Paul's words here. Paul says the man of lawlessness will seat himself in the temple of God, proclaiming himself to be God (2 Thessalonians 2:4). Different building, friend. It's like walking into the bakery next door and asking for my cookies.

Right. Paul asks, "Do you not remember that I told you these things while I was still with you?" (2 Thessalonians 2:5) He's reminding them, not teaching them fresh. They heard it from him when he was with them.

Timothy is a fine guess, since he's one of the three sending the letter (2 Thessalonians 1:1). But Paul says he told them himself: "Do you not remember that I told you these things while I was still with you?" (2 Thessalonians 2:5) So it came straight from Paul.

explanations.answer: They read it in the prophets
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't point them to the prophets here. He says, "Do you not remember that I told you these things while I was still with you?" (2 Thessalonians 2:5) They heard it from him face to face. He's only jogging their memory.

explanations.answer: Until he is taken out of the way
explanations.explanation: That's what Paul says: "…the one who now restrains it will continue until he is taken out of the way." (2 Thessalonians 2:7) The text doesn't say more about who he is or how he's removed. So I'll leave it open, friend, right where the text leaves it.
Paul never ties it to the church growing strong. He says the one who now restrains lawlessness "…will continue until he is taken out of the way." (2 Thessalonians 2:7) That's the only limit he gives.

explanations.answer: Until Paul comes back to visit
explanations.explanation: Paul's visit isn't the marker here. He says the one who restrains it "…will continue until he is taken out of the way." (2 Thessalonians 2:7) Nothing in that verse ties it to Paul coming back.

Yes. Paul says the Lord Jesus will slay the lawless one "…with the breath of His mouth…" and annihilate him "…by the majesty of His arrival." (2 Thessalonians 2:8) There's no battle of equals here. Jesus wins, plain and simple.

This one is actually in the text. Paul says that after the lawless one is revealed, the Lord Jesus will slay him "…with the breath of His mouth…" and annihilate him "…by the majesty of His arrival." (2 Thessalonians 2:8) So the lawless one doesn't get the last word. Jesus does.

Yes, truth is the word, friend. Paul says they perish "…because they refused the love of the truth that would have saved them." (2 Thessalonians 2:10) Refusing the love of the truth is the reason he gives.
The world isn't the word Paul uses. He says those who are perishing refused "…the love of the truth that would have saved them." (2 Thessalonians 2:10) The truth is what they turned down, friend.

The temple came up earlier, when Paul said the man of lawlessness would seat himself in the temple of God (2 Thessalonians 2:4). But that's not what is refused here. Paul says they refused "…the love of the truth that would have saved them." (2 Thessalonians 2:10)
That's the one. Paul says judgment comes upon "…all who have disbelieved the truth and delighted in wickedness." (2 Thessalonians 2:12) The two go together in his words.

Mocking the prophets isn't in Paul's words here. He says judgment comes upon "…all who have disbelieved the truth and delighted in wickedness." (2 Thessalonians 2:12) So the answer is delighting in wickedness.

The Sabbath doesn't come up anywhere in this passage. Paul says judgment will come on those who "…have disbelieved the truth and delighted in wickedness." (2 Thessalonians 2:12) The thing he adds is delighting in wickedness, friend.

That's what Paul says: "…God chose you from the beginning to be saved by the sanctification of the Spirit and by faith in the truth." (2 Thessalonians 2:13) Their salvation was no last-minute thing. God had it in mind from the beginning.
Paul's arrival isn't the timing he gives. He says, "…God chose you from the beginning…" (2 Thessalonians 2:13) The timing he names is from the beginning.

explanations.answer: On the day they were baptized
explanations.explanation: Baptism isn't mentioned in this passage, friend. Paul says, "…God chose you from the beginning to be saved by the sanctification of the Spirit and by faith in the truth." (2 Thessalonians 2:13) The timing he gives is from the beginning.

Yes. Paul says that God chose them "…to be saved by the sanctification of the Spirit and by faith in the truth." (2 Thessalonians 2:13) That's a nice contrast with those who refused the love of the truth (2 Thessalonians 2:10). The Thessalonians are in the group who believed.

It's in the text, friend. Paul says God chose the Thessalonians "…to be saved by the sanctification of the Spirit and by faith in the truth." (2 Thessalonians 2:13) So faith in the truth is part of how they're saved. That sets them apart from those who refused it (2 Thessalonians 2:10).

explanations.answer: To share in the glory of Jesus Christ
explanations.explanation: That's the answer. Paul says God called them through the gospel "…so that you may share in the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ." (2 Thessalonians 2:14) The gospel is how the call reached them, and the glory is what it leads to.

explanations.answer: To be spared from every trouble
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't promise that in these verses. He says God called them "…so that you may share in the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ." (2 Thessalonians 2:14) That's the promise on the table.

explanations.answer: To be honored by every nation
explanations.explanation: Paul never says anything about nations honoring them. He says God called them "…so that you may share in the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ." (2 Thessalonians 2:14) The glory is Jesus', and they get to share in it.

Yes. Paul says, "…stand firm and cling to the traditions we taught you, whether by speech or by letter." (2 Thessalonians 2:15) After all those warnings, he gives them something to do. Plant your feet, friend, and hold on.

Standing back sounds safe, but it isn't what Paul says. He says, "…stand firm and cling to the traditions we taught you, whether by speech or by letter." (2 Thessalonians 2:15) He's calling them to hold their ground, not retreat.

Paul doesn't tell them to stand apart. He says, "…stand firm and cling to the traditions we taught you, whether by speech or by letter." (2 Thessalonians 2:15) Standing apart sounds lonely, and I've had enough of that in my drawer days.

Look at the end of the verse again, friend. Paul says, "…cling to the traditions we taught you, whether by speech or by letter." (2 Thessalonians 2:15) So there were two ways the teaching came, not only speech. A letter counts too.

That's right. Paul says, "…cling to the traditions we taught you, whether by speech or by letter." (2 Thessalonians 2:15) So the teaching came by speech and by letter, not only one of them. Paul wants them to stand firm and cling to it either way.

That's what Paul says. He points to God our Father, "…who by grace has loved us and given us eternal comfort and good hope…" (2 Thessalonians 2:16) Those are the two gifts he names. The comfort is eternal and the hope is good.

Paul doesn't list riches or long life. He points to God our Father, "…who by grace has loved us and given us eternal comfort and good hope…" (2 Thessalonians 2:16) The gifts he names are comfort and hope.

Victory comes up earlier, when Paul says the Lord Jesus will slay the lawless one (2 Thessalonians 2:8). But in this verse, the gifts are different. Paul describes God our Father as the one "…who by grace has loved us and given us eternal comfort and good hope…" (2 Thessalonians 2:16)
